key_insight: Large VLMs often give illusion-consistent answers by recalling learned patterns rather than visually perceiving changes — they frequently keep the same response even when illusion factors are visibly inverted.
problem_solved: Determines whether VLM outputs on classic visual illusions reflect genuine visual perception or memorized associations, and provides a systematic probing framework to separate perception from recall.
method: Construct controlled illusion test sets that include original images and versions with inverted/altered illusion factors.
Probe VLMs with standardized prompts and image manipulations, measuring response invariance and mismatch with human perception.
Quantitatively compare model behaviors across architectures, checkpoints, and prompt variants to isolate memorization vs. perceptual failure.
impact: Provides practitioners a clear evaluation protocol to detect when VLMs rely on memorized patterns instead of processing visual evidence, informing model selection, training, and robustness fixes for multimodal systems.
visual_elements: Side-by-side image pairs (original vs inverted illusion) with model answers and human answers for direct comparison
Pipeline flowchart showing dataset creation → prompting → response analysis → attribution (perception vs recall)
Bar or heatmap chart showing invariance rates across models and prompt conditions
paper_title: Do VLMs Perceive or Recall? Probing Visual Perception vs. Memory with Classic Visual Illusions
paper_authors: Xiaoxiao Sun, Mingyang Li, Kun yuan, Min Woo Sun, Mark Endo
